## Overview

A crop that makes the Bt toxin suppresses its target pest, but the space and
food that pest leaves may go to other pests. @Yang2009 asked how the feeding
of a target pest (the cotton bollworm, B), a secondary pest (a mirid, C) and
their natural enemy (D) shape such a community, with three stacked lattices:

- layer M3 holds the plant A, a quantity in every cell;
- layer M2 holds at most one pest, B or C, in each cell;
- layer M1 holds at most one enemy in each cell;
- in each cycle, individuals move or breed in contiguous pairs of cells; an
  enemy attacks the pest below it, and a pest eats the plant below it, each
  with a probability; individuals that go hungry too long starve.

The Bt toxin enters only as a lower probability that the target pest feeds.
The individuals follow the Penna model of the authors' earlier predator-prey
automaton [@He2002]: they age, carry inherited diseases in a 32-bit genome
and breed from a maturity age.

The source gives the structure but no parameter values, no rule for the plant
and no details of the pairs or the Penna model. This implementation is an
**adaptation**: it takes the individuals from @He2002, chooses the rest
(listed below) and aims at the source's qualitative results.

```{julia}
#| output: false
ENV["GKSwstype"] = "100"
using EcologicalCellularAutomata
using CellularAutomataCore
using Plots
using Statistics
```

## Pairs as a block rule

The source updates "each contiguous pair" of cells on a lattice whose side is
even: an individual next to an empty cell moves into it, or, once mature,
breeds into it. Here the pairs are a random domino tiling: the lattice is cut
into 2 × 2 blocks, the partition shifting by a cell each cycle (the Margolus
scheme), and each block is split into two horizontal or two vertical pairs at
random. Every pair then updates on its own, and so does each cell's predation,
feeding and survival, so the whole cycle is one block rule:

```{julia}
prob = problem(:bt_crop_three_layer; n=100, cycles=600, seed=1)
sol = solve(prob, Margolus(); saveat=0:2:600)
series = bt_crop_summary.(sol.u)
plot(plot(sol.t, [getfield.(series, :B) getfield.(series, :C) getfield.(series, :D)] ./ 100;
          label=["target pest B" "secondary pest C" "enemy D"], ylabel="cells occupied (%)"),
     plot(sol.t, getfield.(series, :plant); label="plant A", ylabel="plant (share of maximum)",
          ylims=(0, 1.05));
     xlabel="cycle", lw=2, layout=(2, 1), size=(750, 520), left_margin=4Plots.mm)
```

With the target pest feeding a little better than the secondary pest (0.6
against 0.5) and enemies catching either with probability 0.6, the target pest
takes over the pest layer within a few hundred cycles, and the enemies settle
on it. The layers at the end:

```{julia}
u = sol.u[end]
plot(heatmap(u.enemy; c=cgrad([:white, :firebrick]), title="M1: enemies D", colorbar=false),
     heatmap(u.pest; c=cgrad([:white, :darkorange, :royalblue], 3; categorical=true),
             title="M2: B (orange), C (blue)", colorbar=false),
     heatmap(u.plant; c=:Greens, clims=(0, 1), title="M3: plant A");
     layout=(1, 3), size=(1000, 320), aspect_ratio=1, ticks=false, titlefontsize=9)
```

## Feeding: the source's Fig. 3

The source swept the two pests' feeding probabilities with the enemy's
predation fixed above one half. Each point here is the mean of the last 100 of
1000 cycles of one run:

```{julia}
function sweep(base, xname, yname; grid=0:0.1:1)
    out = Array{Float64}(undef, length(grid), length(grid), 4)
    Threads.@threads for (i, j) in collect(Iterators.product(eachindex(grid), eachindex(grid)))
        pmap = merge(base, NamedTuple{(xname, yname)}((grid[i], grid[j])))
        integ = init(problem(:bt_crop_three_layer; n=100, cycles=1000, seed=i + 20j, pmap),
                     Margolus(); save_everystep=false)
        acc = zeros(4)
        for t in 1:1000
            step!(integ)
            if t > 900
                s = bt_crop_summary(integ.u)
                acc .+= (s.plant, s.B / 100, s.C / 100, s.D / 100) ./ 100
            end
        end
        out[i, j, :] = acc
    end
    return out
end
function panels(out, xlabel, ylabel; grid=0:0.1:1)
    titles = ["plant A (share)", "target pest B (%)", "secondary pest C (%)", "enemy D (%)"]
    plot([heatmap(grid, grid, permutedims(out[:, :, k]); title=titles[k], xlabel, ylabel,
                  c=k == 1 ? :Greens : :viridis, clims=k == 1 ? (0, 1) : (0, 100))
          for k in 1:4]...; layout=(2, 2), size=(820, 680), titlefontsize=10)
end
fig3 = sweep((; P_DB=0.6, P_DC=0.6), :P_BA, :P_CA)
panels(fig3, "P_BA (B feeds)", "P_CA (C feeds)")
```

As in the source:

- the plant stays near its maximum when the target pest feeds poorly, and
  falls as it feeds better, to about 0.6 when it always feeds (0.65–0.70 in
  the source);
- each pest is absent when it cannot feed, and the secondary pest collapses
  when the target pest feeds better;
- enemies vanish where both pests feed poorly (both probabilities below about
  0.3).

Read along a column, lowering the target pest's feeding (the source's stand-in
for the Bt toxin) hands the pest layer to the secondary pest. Here the switch
is abrupt, once the target pest feeds less well than the secondary pest; in
the source the secondary pest rises more gradually. At P_CA = 0.5:

```{julia}
grid = 0:0.1:1
[(; P_BA=grid[i], B=round(fig3[i, 6, 2]; digits=1), C=round(fig3[i, 6, 3]; digits=1))
 for i in 1:2:11]
```

## Predation: the source's Fig. 4

The source then swept the enemy's predation of the two pests, with the target
pest the better feeder:

```{julia}
fig4 = sweep((; P_BA=0.6, P_CA=0.5), :P_DB, :P_DC)
panels(fig4, "P_DB (D eats B)", "P_DC (D eats C)")
```

As in the source:

- enemies that catch the target pest well and the secondary pest with
  probability about 0.2 to 0.5 release the secondary pest, which then fills
  most of the pest layer;
- enemies that catch the secondary pest better than the target pest hold it
  down;
- enemies that catch the target pest well die out when they catch the
  secondary pest with probability below about 0.2; they remove the target
  pest and starve, as in the source, though here the target pest then returns;
- the plant is highest where the enemies hold both pests down.

This is the source's warning: suppressing a primary pest, by an enemy or a
toxin, can let a secondary pest break out.

## What is not reproduced

In the source the two pests share the pest layer over most of both sweeps:
about 80,000 and 105,000 of 250,000 cells with no predation at all. Here the
better feeder excludes the other, as two consumers of one resource in the same
cells are expected to; no plant setting tried let them coexist. It follows
that:

- without enemies, the target pest feeds alone and the plant falls to about
  0.5, where the source keeps it at about 0.92;
- enemies that catch the target pest with probability below about 0.4 die
  out here even when they catch the secondary pest well, since that pest has
  been excluded; for the same reason the plant does not rise to its maximum
  when enemies catch the secondary pest well;
- enemies occupy about 20–26% of cells, against 10–17% in the source.

The source's coexistence must come from something it does not report, such as
different life histories for the two pests, or runs too short for exclusion.
